summary: God’s settled opposition to sin, not a flaw in his character but the necessary corollary of his holiness; central to understanding the cross
readingInstruction: Read Romans 1:18-32 again, and then Nahum 1:2-8. Today is a doctrinal pause on the wrath of God. The question is simple and hard: how can a God of love be angry? Read slowly, and notice that Nahum holds wrath and goodness together in the same breath.
settingTheScene: Many people are uneasy with the idea that God is angry. Some picture the God of the Old Testament as wrathful and the God of the New as gentle, but the New Testament speaks of wrath at least as often as the Old. Paul says it is the first thing “revealed” in the gospel’s unfolding (Romans 1:18). The prophet Nahum, writing perhaps a century after Jonah, announces judgment on Nineveh, the same city that repented under Jonah and later returned to cruelty. Together the two passages give us a biblical view of divine opposition to sin.
observation: “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men” (Romans 1:18).
“Therefore God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to impurity” (Romans 1:24).
“For this reason God gave them up to dishonorable passions” (Romans 1:26).
“God gave them up to a debased mind to do what ought not to be done” (Romans 1:28).
“The LORD is a jealous and avenging God; the LORD is avenging and wrathful” (Nahum 1:2).
“The LORD is slow to anger and great in power, and the LORD will by no means clear the guilty” (Nahum 1:3).
“Who can stand before his indignation? Who can endure the heat of his anger?” (Nahum 1:6).
“The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; he knows those who take refuge in him” (Nahum 1:7).
doctrinalFocus:
The wrath of God is his settled, holy, and righteous opposition to all evil. It is not a loss of temper. Human anger is often selfish, sudden, and out of control. God’s wrath is none of these. It flows from his holiness and his love of what is good. A God who did not hate injustice, cruelty, and the destruction of his creatures would not be good. If we love victims, we should want a God who is angry at what harms them.

Scripture describes wrath in at least two ways. In Romans 1, wrath is revealed in the present, as God gives people over to the consequences of their own choices: sin becomes its own punishment. And elsewhere wrath is future: Paul speaks of a “day of wrath when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed” (Romans 2:5). Nahum shows God’s wrath as both patient and certain: “slow to anger,” yet he “will by no means clear the guilty.”

The wrath of God is the background that makes the gospel good news. At the cross, Jesus bore this wrath for his people. The word “propitiation” (Romans 3:25) means a sacrifice that turns away wrath. Christians have debated the word, but its main meaning is clear: God’s justice and God’s love meet at the cross, where the Son absorbs what sin deserves. Therefore, for the believer, “there is now no condemnation” (Romans 8:1). Nahum 1:7 is the comfort: “The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; he knows those who take refuge in him.” The same God who is a fire to his enemies is a refuge to those who run to him. Christians differ on how to describe the final punishment of the unrepentant, but all agree that God’s judgment is just.
interpretation:
Paul says wrath “is revealed from heaven.” It is not a mere theory; it is evident in the moral order of the world. Then he describes its form three times: “God gave them up.” Notice the pattern. People suppress the truth, and God gives them up to impurity (verse 24). They exchange the truth about God for a lie, and God gives them up to dishonorable passions (verse 26). They do not see fit to acknowledge God, and God gives them up to a debased mind (verse 28). The result is a downward spiral. Sin is not merely breaking rules; it is worship turned the wrong way. When we will not worship the Creator, we worship the creature, and the creature cannot bear the weight.

Nahum brings the other side of the picture. The prophet opens with a hymn to the character of God. “The LORD is a jealous and avenging God.” Jealous here means that he will not share his glory or his people with idols, as a husband is rightly jealous for his wife. “Slow to anger and great in power,” a phrase that echoes Exodus 34:6-7. Slow to anger means patience, not weakness. Nineveh had been given time and a prophet. But patience has an end. Mountains quake before him, and the earth heaves. “Who can stand before his indignation?”

Then, in the middle of the storm, the verse that changes the tone: “The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; he knows those who take refuge in him.” There are only two kinds of people before this God: those who stand against him and those who take refuge in him. The gospel is the invitation to refuge. Jesus is the place where the storm has already broken. Wrath fell on him at Calvary so that it would not fall on us.

When we say we are unsettled by the wrath of God, we do well to ask what it would mean for him not to be angry at evil. Paul teaches that the cure for our unease is not to quiet the doctrine but to run to the cross.
connection: Exodus 34:6-7 describes the character of God with mercy and justice. Psalm 7:11 says God is angry with the wicked every day. John 3:36 speaks of the wrath of God remaining on those who do not believe. Romans 2:5, 5:9, and 1 Thessalonians 1:10 speak of wrath to come and our deliverance. Romans 3:25 and 1 John 4:10 speak of propitiation. Hebrews 12:28-29 says our God is a consuming fire. Jonah 3 to 4 is the earlier chapter of Nineveh’s story. Revelation 6:15-17 describes the wrath of the Lamb.
application:
Ask where you have been tempted to soften what Scripture says about God’s wrath, and why.

If you are afraid of God’s judgment, take refuge in Christ today. Say the words of Nahum 1:7 as a prayer.

Pray for someone you love who does not yet see their need of a Savior.
prayerPrompts: Confess where you have wanted a God without wrath.
Ask him to teach you to see his wrath and his mercy together.
Thank Jesus for bearing wrath for you.
